Setting up of Disability Rehabilitation Centres in Madhya Pradesh  
†*61. SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: Will the Minister of SOC IAL JUSTICE AND 
EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a)  whether it is a fact that there is a proposal for setting up of Disability Rehabilitation 
Centres for the disabled persons in every district; 
(b)  whether these Centres have been set-up in only 17 districts of Madhya Pradesh till date 
and if so, by when the permission for setting up these Centres in the remaining districts would be 
given; and 
(c) by when the financial assistance/grant would be sanctioned for setting up of sufficient 
number of these Centres keeping in view that there are 14 lakh disabled persons in the 
State and the present arrangement is adequate for them? 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

2    Oral Answers                    [2 MARCH, 2008]                         to Questions  
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI 
MEIRA KUMAR):  (a) to (c) Statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
Statement  
(a)  No Madam, District Disability Rehabilitation Centres (DDRCs) are set up in unserved 
districts only. 
(b)  Twenty Two DDRCs have already been set up in Madhya Pradesh. Setting up of any 
additional DDRCs in States are dependent on the intrinsic need and other related issues. 
(c)  Keeping in view the need and other issues, grants-in-aid are sanctioned for setting up 
of DDRCs from time to time.

Swadhar Shelter Homes Scheme  
*65. DR . GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister of WOMEN AN D CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
91  the objective and genesis of Swadhar Shelter Homes Scheme; 
92  the progress/achievements thereof till date, particularly in Rajasthan; and 
93  the number of widows, divorced, separated women, both in rural and urban areas, rehabilitated, out 
of 342.90 lakh widowed women and 23.43 lakh divorce d or separated women in the country, as per 
2001 census? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House  

10    Oral Answers  [RAJYA SABHA]  to Questions  
Statement  
(a) Swadhar Scheme has been designed with flexible and innovative approach to cater to 
the requirement of various categories of women in distress under difficult conditions. It was 
introduced in the year 2001-02. The objective of Swadhar Scheme are:—  
91  To provide primary need of shelter, food, clothing and care to the marginalized 
women/ girls living in difficult circumstances who are without any social and economic 
support; 
92  To provide emotional support and counseling to such women; 
93  To rehabilitate them socially and economically through education, awareness, skill 
upgradation and personality development through behavioral training etc.; 
94  To arrange for specific clinical, legal and other support for women/girls in need of 
those intervention by linking and networking with o ther organizations in both 
Government and non-Government sectors on case to case basis; 
95  To provide Help-line or other facilities to such women in distress; and 
96  To provide such other services as will be required for support and rehabilitation to 
such women in distress. 
 
91  As on date, under Swadhar Scheme, 210 Shelter Homes  including 2 
Shelter Homes in Rajasthan and 210 Women Help-lines  have been sanctioned 
across the country. 
92  13,238 destitute women irrespective of whether they  are 
divorced/separated/widowed, have benefited under Sw adhar Shelter Homes 
Scheme since the inception of this Scheme.

Reservation benefits to dalit christians and muslims  
*66. PROF. P.J. KURIEN: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
be pleased to state:  
91  whether dalit christians and muslims have asked for reservation benefits; 
92  if so, the details thereof; and 
93  the reaction of Government to their demand? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MEIRA 
KUMAR): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the table of the House.  
(a) to (c) There have been demands from various quarters to specify the Scheduled Castes 
converted to Christianity as well as Islam, as Scheduled Castes. The government expanded 
the terms of reference of the National Commission for Religious and Linguistic Minorities 
so that it could include its recommendations on the  subject. Further, Civil Writ Petitions 
have been filed in the Supreme Court, wherein it has been prayed to declare clause (3) of the 
Constitution (Scheduled Castes( Order, 1950 as unconstitutional and void as also the denial 
of benefits to them. Petitions has also been filed in High Courts of Bombay, Madras, Jammu 
& Kashmir, Punjab & Haryana and Rajasthan. The matter is presently subjudice.  
PROF. P.J. KURIEN: Sir, perhaps, the hon. Minister was aware of this ruling in advance. 
That is why she has given a crisp answer, but also evasive answer. So, Sir, the hon. Minister 
has not given a directly reply. In any case, she ha s mentioned that the Government has 
expanded the Terms of Reference of the National Commission for Religious and Linguistic 
Minorities so that it could include its recommendations of the subject. I would like to know 
whether the Commission has submitted its recommendations to the Government. Now, if the 
Government has received its recommendations, I woul d like to know whether they have  

Oral Answers  [3 MARCH, 2008]  to Questions    15  
implemented the same. Secondly, is there any commit tee, which the Government has appointed, for a 
study to be made on the relative backwardness of these most backward people?  
SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR: Sir, so far as the National C ommission for Religious and Linguistic 
Minorities is concerned, its Terms of Reference was expanded to consider whether Dalit Christians and 
Dalit Muslims could be treated at par with the Sche duled Castes and could be given reservations. They 
have submitted their Report. In their recommendations, they have stated that para (3) of the Constitution 
(Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950 should be deleted so as to completely delink the Scheduled Castes status 
from religion. This is the recommendation of the Na tional Commission for Religious and Linguistic 
Minorities. Apart from that, there is also a high-level committee appointed by the Prime Minister.  
And they have also said that we cannot equate Arzal  and Ajlaf Muslims, that one is much more 
backward than the other and should be included in t he most backward class of OBCs becaue they are 
mosre or less at par in their occupation with the S cheduled Castes. Now, so far as the National 
Commission for Scheduled Castes is concerned, it is  mandatory for us to take their advice, seek their 
recommendations, on all issues pertaining to the Scheduled Castes. So, we had referred this matter to the 
Commission and they have given their report saying that the reservations should be extended to them, that 
is, to the Dalit Christians and Dalit Muslims. But the share of 15 per cent of SCs should not be disturbed 
and they element of reservation for these communities should be determined by the Government keeping 
in view their population, and, as per the direction of the Supreme Court, the overall reservation of 50 per 
cent has to be maintained.  
Now, when the National Commission for Backward Clas ses was set up through an Act, it became 
mandatory that all issues concerning OBCs be referred to it. Now, the Christians and the Muslims fall in 
the category of Other Backward Classes and till ow they are the subject matter of the National 
Commission for Backward Classes. So, the matter has been referred to them for their recommendation 
and advice.  
PROF. P.J. KURIEN: Sir, it is not the question of a  particular religion or community; it is really a 
question of backwardness. It is the declared policy  of the Government and it is also mentioned in our 
Constitution that Government can enact laws and bri ng in special measures for the upliftment of the 
backward and most backward classes. In view of all the reports already read by the hon. Minister now in 
this House, and in view of the fact that relatively  these people are perhaps more backward than others , 
will the Government take a positive attitude towards this genuine problem?  
SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR: Sir, I have given all the details. Right in the beginning, I had to choose 
between being crisp and being lengthy. I am afraid, I had to choose the second option and I gave in a very 
long reply all the details. The matter is under a v ery detailed consultation process which is mandatory by 
law and also by Constitution. We certainly cannot circumvent that.

DR. M.S. GILL: Sir, caste oppression in the country  is known to all. It is also accepted that it would  
continue for long, perhaps, far into the century. Three faiths in my knowledge— Christianity first, th en 
Islam, then Sikhism—tried to fight this caste busin ess. I think, none of them succeeded; Sikhism, 
certainly has not. This question of giving benefits to those who are oppressed by other castes, whethe r 
they are of this faith or that, was taken up by the  Sikhs immediately after Independence. I think, it took 
30 years to give them reservation. Finally, this country gave them reservation. It is illogical, perhaps, but 
it was given. I do not see why Christians and Musli ms also should not be treated similarly. I would 
request the Minister not to allow Commissions and c ourts to stand as barriers and to fight it. Finally , I

WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS  
Power crisis  
*62. DR. ABHISHEK MANU SINGHVI: Will the Minister o f POWER be pleased to 
state:  
90.  whether Government is aware that many States in the  country are facing a major 
power crisis which, in turn, is hampering their development in a major way; 
91.  if so, what efforts are being made in co-ordination with the affected State Governments 
to rectify the situation; 
92.  whether a timeframe has been set to address the problem; and 
93.  if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): ( a) and (b) There 
is continuing overall shortage of power in the coun try. The quantum of shortage varies 
from State to State on day to day and hour to hour depending on demand and supply of 
power. The energy and peak shortage in the country during the current year (April, 2007 
to January, 2008) was 9% and 15.2% respectively. Th e State-wise power supply position 
during January, 2008 as well as for the period April, 2007 to January, 2008 is given in the 
Statement-I and II (See below).  
Electricity is a concurrent subject under the constitution. The supply and distribution of 
electricity in the State/UT is within the purview o f the respective State Government/State 
Power Utility. The Government of India supplements the efforts of State Governments by 
establishing power plants in the cental sector through Central Public Sector Undertakings.  
The following steps have been taken/are being taken to improve power supply position in 
the country:  
(i) Augmentation of generating capacity by over 78,000 M W is proposed in the eleventh 
Plan.  
(ii) Development of Ultra Mega Power Projects of 4,000 M W capacity each under tariff 
based competitive bidding.  
(iii) "Partnership in Excellence" Programme starting with adoption of better operation 
and maintenance (O&M) practices to enable enhancement of Plant Load Factor (PLF)

of existing thermal power stations through tie-up with well performing power utilities 
as a pre-cursor to renovation and modernization.  
(iv) Renovation, modernization and life extension of old and inefficient generating units.  
(v) Harnessing surplus captive power into the grid. 
(vi) Coordinated operation and maintenance of hydro, thermal, nuclear and gas based 
power stations to optimally utilize the existing generation capacity.  
(vii) Strengthening of inter-state and inter-regional transmission capacity for optimum 
utilization of available power.  
(viii) Promoting demand side management, energy efficiency and energy conservation 
measures.  
(ix) Monitoring of production, transportation and supply of coal to major thermal power 
stations in the country to review and resolve the constraints.  
(x) Import of coal to bridge the gap between anticipated demand and domestic production 
of coal.  
(xi) Import of power from Bhutan.  
Ministry of Power has been closely monitoring and i nteracting through 
meetings/ discussions with the State Governments as well as State Power Utilities for giving 
an impetus to various measures for reducing shortage of power. The first conference of Chief 
Secretaries/ Power Secretaries of various States/UTs was held on 23rd-24th April, 2007 to 
resolve various issues related to the eleventh Plan projects and to ensure the large capacity 
addition during the Plan. This was followed by the Chief Ministers' Conference on power 
sector issues which was presided over by the Hon'bl e Prime Minister on 28th May, 2007. 
Thereafter, the Ministry of Power and the Central E lectricity Authority organized an 
International Conclave on 4th & 5th July, 2007 on " Key inputs for accelerated 
development of power sector for eleventh Plan and b eyond" in order to ensure 
availability of key inputs and material for timely implementation of eleventh Plan projects. 
A meeting of the Group of Ministers, chaired by Min ister of Power was held on 24th 
September, 2007. During the meeting, a Task Force o n Hydro Project Developmet and a 
Sub-Committee of Group of Ministers' to look into f inancing issues, particularly for 
upgradation of transmission and distribution were c onstituted and detailed State-wise 
discussions were held with regard to accelerated power generation capacity addition for the 
eleventh Plan. Subsequently, a follow up meeting of Chief Secretaries of the States was held 
on 19th February, 2008, wherein completion of order ing of all the eleventh Plan projects 
by the end of March, 2008, reduction of Aggregate T echnical and Commercial (AT&C) 
losses, implementation of Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana, implementation of 
open access in transmission and distribution, strengthening of transmission systems in the 
State Sector were discussed in detail.  
(c) and (d) The National Electricity Policy envisag es "Power for All by 2012" and per 
capita availability of power to be increased to over 1000 units by 2011-12. To achieve this 
objective, a total capacity additon of over 78,000 MW is required during the eleventh Plan 
period.

Development of Food Processing Industries  
312. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of FOOD PROCESSING INDUSTRIES 
be pleased to state:  
 whether the country still lags behind many countrie s in food processing and food 
packaging industries; 
 if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
 the steps proposed to be taken by Government for the development of food processing 
industries in the country particularly the processi ng of Indian food varieties on modern 
lines? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF FOOD PROCE SSING 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI SUBODH KANT SAHAY): (a) to (c) India's food processing sector 
has a huge potential for development. However, its present level of processing is extremely 
low. For example, the level of processing is 2.2% for fruits and vegetables, 26% for marine, 
6% for poultry and 20% for buffalo meat, as against 60-70% in developed countries. India's 
export of processed food in global trade is only 1.5%.  
In order to address the low level of processing and to promote food processing industries 
to exploit both the domestic and international market potential for processed food products, 
a Vision Document 2015 on Food Processing Industries for the country as a whole has been 
finalized by the Ministry of Food Processing Indust ries (MFPI), which envisages trebling 
the size of the processed food sector by increasing  the level of processing of perishables 
from 6% to 20%, value addition from 20% to 35% and share in global food trade from 1.5% 
to 3% by 2015. An integrated strategy for promotion  of agribusiness-Vision, Strategy and 
Action Plan for the Food Processing Sector has also been approved by the Government.  
The thrust areas identified for strategic intervention include establishment of Mega Food 
Parks in identified clusters with appropriate backw ard and forward linkages, creation of 
integrated cold chains/value addition and preservat ion infrastructure, modernization of 
abattoirs, upgradation of hygiene and quality of street food and food streets, establishment 
and upgradation of quality control laboratories, re structuring and strengthening of MFPI, 
rationalizing tax structure, incentivising FDI and private investment in infrastructure,

undertaking capacity building of small and unorgani zed sector, liberalized wine and beer 
policy, launching a major promotional campaign for the food processing sector and larger 
public investment for creation of critical rural infrastructure in food processing sector.  
The Ministry has been implementing various other sc hemes also for promotion and 
development of food processing industries. Under the Scheme for Technology Upgradation/ 
Modernization/Establishment of Food Processing Industries, Ministry of Food Processing 
Industries extends financial assistance to food processing units in the form of grants-in-aid 
@ 25% of the cost of plant and machinery and technical civil works subjects to a maximum 
of Rs. 50.00 lakhs in general areas or 33.33% subje ct to maximum of Rs. 75.00 lakhs in 
difficult areas such as Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal  Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and 
North Eastern States, A & N Islands, Lakshadweep and ITDP Areas. In addition, under the 
Technology Mission for Integrated Development of Ho rticulture in North Eastern State, 
Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, higher levels of assistance @50% 
of the eligible components upto Rs. 4.00 crore for setting up and Rs. 1.00 crore for upgradation 
of fruit and vegetables processing is allowed. The Government of India has also launched 
the National Horticulture Mission (NHM) for holisti c development of Horticulture in the 
country. Financial assistance in the form of grant-in-aid is also provided for Development of 
Infrastructure, Human Resource Development, Promotion of Quality Assurance, Laboratories, 
Codex Standards and R&D and other promotional measu res to encourage development of 
the food processing industries.  
Expansion of Food Processing Industries  
313. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of F OOD PROCESSING 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state:  
 whether it is a fact that the food processing indus tries despite being priority sector, 
has not flourished to its potential for various reasons; 
 whether it is also a fact that most significant among them are the unfavourable legal 
regime governing food products and agricultural marketing and the lack of vital infrastructure, 
notably cold chains; and 
 if so, the steps Government proposes to take to promote rapid expansion of this sector 
to avert huge wastage of perishable food? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF FOOD PROCE SSING 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI SUBODH KANT SAHAY): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. India with its strong 
base in agriculture provides a large and varied raw  material base for food processing. The 
total food consumption in India is estimated at Rs. 860,000 crores of which consumption of 
processed food accounts for Rs. 460,000 crores. Further, with liberalization of global trade 
regime, India has the opportunity to export more processed food items to international markets. 
The growth rate of food processing industries durin g the 9th Plan period has been 7.1%. 
The average rate of growth during the first four ye ars of the 10th Plan was @13.025% at 
current prices and @6.75% at 1999-2000 prices. Ther e has been significant growth of 
food processing units during the last three-four ye ars. During the period 2003-2004 to 
2006-2007 growth of Food Processing units in the small scale sector has registered an increase 
of 21% from 16.5 lakhs to 20 lakh units. Further, F DI in FPI sector has increased from 
Rs. 177 crores in 2002-03 to Rs. 441 crores in 2006 -07.  

Written Answers to  [3 MARCH, 2008]  Unstarred Questions   43  
The food processing sector has therefore, shown considerable growth during the last four 
years. However, there is still considerable potenti al that exist for the growth of the food 
processing sector. Some of the major constraints in the growth of food processing industries 
include lack of required infrastructure facilities such as farm level primary processing centres, 
collection centres, storage facilities, cold chain and transportation system of farm products 
from farm to market and processing centres, lack of backward and forward linkages and low 
capacity utilization of units, etc. It also included the existence of multiplicity of Food Laws 
and standard setting and enforcement agencies and unfavourable tax regime.  
In order to address these constraints and to promote food processing industries to exploit 
both the domestic and international market potentia l, a Vision Document 2015 on Food 
Processing Industries for the country as a whole has been finalized by the Ministry of Food 
Processing Industries (MFPI), which envisages trebling the size of the processed food sector . 
by increasing the level of Processing of perishable  from 6% to 20%, value addition from 
20% to 35% and share in global food trade from 1.5% to 3% by 2015. The Government has 
approved the integrated strategy for promotion of agribusiness-Vision, Strategy and Action 
Plan for the Food Processing Sector.  
During the Tenth Plan the Ministry has been providing financial assistance in the form of 
grant for setting up of Food Parks under its Plan S cheme @25% of project cost in general 
areas and @33.33% in difficult areas subject to a maximum of Rs. 4 crores for creation of 
common facilities such as power, water supply, cold  storage, food testing labs, common 
processing facilities, effluent treatment plant, et c. It has also been providing grant-in-aid 
upto 25% of cost of plant and machinery and technic al civil works in general areas and 
33.33% in difficult areas with a ceiling of Rs. 75 lakhs for setting up of cold storages including 
special type of cold storages with controlled/modified atmosphere technology as an integral 
part of processing units or as a common facility in food parks for non-horticulture produces.  
The thrust areas identified for strategic intervention cover, establishment of Mega Food 
Parks in identified clusters with appropriate backw ard and forward linkages, creation of 
integrated cold chains/value addition and preservat ion infrastructure, modernization of 
abattoirs, upgradation of hygienic and quality stre et food and food streets, establishment 
and upgradation of quality control laboratories, re structuring and strengthening of MFPI, 
rationalizing lax structure, incentivising FDI and private investment in infrastructure, 
undertaking capacity building of small and unorganized sector, launching a major promotional 
campaign for the food processing sector and need for larger public investment for creation 
of critical rural infrastructure in food processing sector.  
In the 11 th Plan, the Ministry proposes to implement a revamped Scheme for Infrastructure 
Development under which, it will give financial ass istance for setting up of Mega Food 
Parks, cold chain infrastructure, value added centres and packaging centres. The Mega Food 
Park Scheme will provide backward and forward linkages as well as reliable and sustainable 
supply chain. The Cluster based demand driven approach will provide linkages from farm to 
market with linkages from local to regional level t hrough Primary Processing Centres, 
Collection Centres, Strategic Distribution Centre-c um-Cold Chain at critical locations— 
having Controlled Atmosphere storage and distribution centres where large quantities can 
be stored and supplied to distribution centres for fresh sale, and to processing industries for 
processing. The emphasis will be on building strong linkages with agriculture and horticulture, 
enhancing project implementation capabilities, incr eased involvement of private sector 
investment and support for creation of rural infrastructure to ensure a steady supply of good

quality agri horticulture produce. As in the Tenth plan, in the Eleventh plan also under the 
Scheme for Technology Upgradation/Modernization/Est ablishment of Food Processing 
Industries, Ministry of Food Processing Industries extending financial assistance to food 
processing units in the form of grants-in-aid @25% of the cost of plan and machinery and 
technical civil works subject to a maximum of Rs. 50.00 lakhs in general areas or 33.33% 
subject to maximum of Rs. 75.00 lakhs in difficult areas.  
In regard to the multiplicity of Food Laws and enfo rcement agencies governing food 
products, the Government has notified an integrated  Food Safety and Standard Act, 2006 
which envisages establishment of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India for laying 
down science based standards for articles of food and to regulate their manufacturer, storage,

Statement  
Extracts from the "Compilation of Recommendations on Education"  
"4. Regulation  
There is a clear need to establish an Independent R egulatory Authority for Higher 
Education (IRAHE). Such a regulatory authority is both necessary and desirable.  
It is necessary for two important reasons. First, in India, it requires an Act of Legislature of 
Parliament to set up a University. The deemed university route is much too difficult for new 
institutions. Entry through legislation alone, as a t present, is a formidable barrier. The 
consequence is a steady increase in the average size of existing universities with a steady 
deterioration in their quality. The absence of competition only compounds problems. Second, as we 
seek to expand the higher education system, entry norms will be needed for private institutions 
and public-private partnerships. The institutional framework for this purpose must be put in 
place here and now.  
It is desirable for four important reasons. First, it would minimize conflicts of interest as it would 
create an arm's length distance from stakeholders. Second, it would replace the present system 
which is over-regulated but under-governed, through more appropriate forms of intervention. Third, it 
would rationalize the existing system where mandates are both confusing and overlapping. Fourth, 
it would dispense with the multiplicity or regulatory agencies to provide a single-window 
clearance.  
The present regulatory system in higher education is flawed in many respects. The barriers to 
entry are too high. The system of authorizing entry is cumbersome and there are extensive rules 
after entry, as the UGC seeks to regulate almost every aspect of an institution from fees to 
curriculum... The other regulators, say in the sphe re of professional education, are often 
inconsistent in their adherence to principles. There are several instances where an engineering 
college or a business school is approved, promptly, in a small house of a metropolitan suburb 
without the requisite teachers, infrastructure or f acilities, but established universities 
experience difficulties in obtaining similar approvals. Such examples can be multiplied. These 
would only confirm that the complexity, the multiplicity and the rigidity of the existing regulatory 
structure is not conducive to the expansion of higher education opportunities in India.  
In sum, the existing regulatory framework constraints the supply of good institutions, 
excessively regulates existing institutions in the wrong places, and is not conducive to 
innovation or creativity in higher education. The challenge is therefore to design a regulatory 
system that increases the supply of good institutio ns and fosters accountability in those 
institutions. An independent regulator has to be the cornerstone of such a system.  
The proposed IRAHE will rationalize the principles on which entry is regulated. There are 
two aspects to this rationalization: what is to be regulated and what are the principles used for 
regulation.  

Written Answers to  [3 MARCH, 2008]  Unstarred Questions   53  
In higher education, regulators perform five functions: (1) Entry: licence to grant degrees. 
(2) Accreditation: quality benchmarking. (3) Disbursement of public funds. (4) Access: fees 
or affirmative action. (5) Licence: to practice pro fession.  
India is perhaps the only country in the world where regulation in four of the five function , 
is carried out by one entity, that is, the UGC. The  purpose of creating an IRAHE is to 
separate these functions. The proposed IRAHE shall be responsible for setting the criteria 
and deciding on entry. It would, in addition, licen se agencies to take care of accreditation. 
The role of the UGC will be limited to disbursing p ublic funds, Issues of access will be 
governed by State legislation on reservation and ot her forms of affirmative action. And, 
professional association may, in some institutions,  set requirements to determine eligibility 
for conducting a profession. All other regulatory agencies such as the AICTE will need to be 
abolished while the MCI and the BCI will be limited to their role as professional associations. 
These professional associations could conduct natio nwide examinations to provide licence 
for those wishing to enter the profession. 
The second aspect of regulation is the principle use to regulate. The IRAHE will determine 
eligibility for setting up a new institution based on transparent criteria rafter than discretionary 
controls. Its main role would be to exercise due diligence at the point it approves a licence to 
grant degrees. In doing so, it would assess the academic credibility and the financial viability 
of the proposed institution on the basis of informa tion submitted in accordance with the 
stipulated criteria. It will apply exactly the same  norms to public and private institutions, 
just as it will apply the same norms to domestic and international institutions.  
The IRAHE would have to be established by an Act of Parliament. It would be the only 
agency that would be authorized to accord degree gr anting power to higher education 
institutions. It would also be responsible for monitoring standards and settling disputes. It 
should also be thought of as the authority for licensing accreditation agencies. The IRAHE 
must be at an arm's-length from the government and independent of all stakeholders including 
the concerned Ministries of the Government. The Act s of the UGC, AICTE, MCI and 
BCI would have to be amended. The role of the UGC would be re-defined to focus on the 
disbursement of grants to, and maintenance of, public institutions in higher education. The 
entry regulatory functions of the AICTE, the MCI and the BCI would be performed by the 
IRAHE, so that their role would be limited to that of professional associations. These 
professional associations could conduct nationwide examinations to provide licences for 
those wishing to enter the profession."

Criteria for opening Kendriya Vidyalayas and Navoda ya Vidyalayas  
340. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA:  
SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI:  
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
 the criteria for opening Kendriya Vidyalayas and Navodaya Vidyalayas in a State; 
 whether the above criteria have been strictly adhered to in Rajasthan; 
 if so, the number of such schools in Rajasthan; 
 total number of students in these schools, as on date; 
 whether there is a huge shortage of trained teachers in these schools; 
 if so, the steps taken by Government to meet the shortage; and 
 whether there is any reservation for SC/ST/OBC girls and whether it has been fully 
availed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESO URCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) Opening of a Kendriya Vidyalaya 
depends upon receipt of a viable proposal from the sponsor i.e. State Government/Public  

Written Answers to  [3 MARCH, 2008]  Unstarred Questions   63  
Sector Undertakings etc. committing free land and t emporary accommodation, availability 
of adequate number of students of specified categor ies, approval of the competent authority 
and availability of funds, etc. Opening of a Jawaha r Navodaya Vidyalaya (JNV) is based on 
receipt of a viable proposal from the concerned Sta te/UT Government offering suitable land 
 free of cost along with provision of temporary building till the construction of permanent  
building. The present scheme of Navodaya Vidyalaya envisages one Vidyalaya per district.  
 Kendriya Vidyalayas (KVs) in the State of Rajasthan have been opened as per the prescribed 
norms except for 03 schools that were opened during the years 2003-04 and 2004-05. 
 At present, there are 57 KVs and 32 JNVs in the State of Rajasthan. 
 As on date, there are 53,711 students in KVs and 14 ,884 students in JNVs in the State of 
Rajasthan. 
 In the State of Rajasthan, 255 posts of teachers in KVs and 89 posts of teachers in JNVs are lying 
vacant. These constitute 12.62% and 11.74% respectively of the sanctioned strengths in KVs and JNVs 
of Rajasthan. 
 Filling up of vacant posts is a continuous process. Whenever there are vacancies that cannot be 
filled up immediately by regular recruitment, suitable persons are engaged on part time/contract basis to 
safeguard the academic interest of the students. 
 (g) Seats are reserved for children from SC/ST Community in proportion to the population  
in the concerned State/district but not less than the national average of 15% for Scheduled Caste and 7.5% 
for Scheduled Tribe Communities. In JNVs of Rajasthan, 24.5% of enrolment pertains to SC and 16.14% of 
enrolment pertains to ST. The reserved seats have not been fully availed of in Kendriya Vidyalayas. 
Whenever enough SC/ST students are not available for admission till a cut off date of academic session, the 
vacant seats for SC are offered to ST and vice versa. Seats remaining vacant thereafter get de-
reserved.

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESO URCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) and (b ) According to a 2007 
World Bank study "Unleashing India's Innovation: Towards Sustainable and Inclusive Growth",

national corporations and partly by blossoming of India's IT and IT-enabled service sectors.

education. The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) has also an All India Board of 
Studies in Information Technology, which advises the Council on, inter-alia, the model curricula 
for IT courses and their upgradation. Besides, a programme of Finishing School for unemployed 
engineering graduates, so as to prepare them for the IT/ ITeS Industries, has been taken up 
since 2007-08.

increase the skilled workforce in the country:

from Government of India whereas 400 ITIs with the assistance from the World Bank.  
(ii) Upgradation of remaining 1396 Government Industrial Training Institutes under Public 
Private Partnership.  
(iii) A scheme under the title "Skill Development Initiative" has also been taken up to impart 
short term Modular Employable Skills under which 231 short term courses have been 
developed.

streams and vocational courses including IT-related courses at the higher secondary level for skill 
development.

ITEM NO. 2   INFRASTRUCTURE OF SUBORDINATE COURTS  
ITEM NO. 7   MODERNISATION OF COURTS  
Some Chief Justices drew attention of the Chief Min isters of their respective states to the 
inadequate infrastructure, such as dilapidated cour t buildings, lack'of esential amenities 
and frequent power failures, particularly at Taluka level. All the States acknowledged the 
need to replace the old and dilapidated court build ings by standardized modern court 
buildings, add more court rooms to the existing cou rt buildings and construct more court 
complexes and residential quarters for Judicial Off icers. Some Chief Ministers wanted 
allocation of adequate funds to them by Central Gov ernment for augmenting the 
infrastructure of subordinate courts. The Hon'ble U nion Minister for Law and Justice 
informed that Government of India was committed to give full support to the States for 
construction of court buildings and judges residenc es under a Ten Year Perspective 
Plan  
DECISION  
 Consistent with the resources available to them, th e States will provide adequate 
funds, as required by the High Court, for upgrading  and augmenting the infrastructure of 
subordinate courts by replacing the dilapidated bui ldings with new buildings, upgrading 
the existing court complexes and constructing new c ourt complexes and residential 
quarters for judicial officers. 
 Adequate steps be taken for modernization & computerisation of courts and enhancing 
the use of various I.T. tools including video confe rencing, Internet usage, E-mail based 
communication, electronic dissemination of informat ion and use of digital signatures, 
particularly at the level of subordinate courts. 
ITEM NO. 3    ENHANCING THE STRENGTH OF JUDGES AND REDUCTION OF 
ARREARS  
ITEM NO . 6.   FAST TRACK COURTS  
All the chief justices highlighted the inadequate j udge case ratio in their respective 
States and wanted increase in existing sanctioned s trength of subordinate judges by 
atleast 25%. No participant disputed that the huge pendency of cases in the courts 
cannot be wiped out unless the strength of judges i n High Courts as well as subordinate 
courts was suitably enhanced. The States acknowledg ed the acute shortage of 
subordinate judges and the need to increase their number adequately so as to enable them 
to reduce backlog and provide an efficient, speedy and effective justice delivery system to 
our people. The States also stressed on the need to  fill-up the existing vacancies in 
subordinate courts as well as High Courts at an early date and felt that the arrears could 
come down substantially if all the existing vacancies were filled on urgent basis.

Some Chief Justices pointed out that there was huge pendency of civil cases as well, 
both in High Courts as well as in subordinate Court s and many of these cases were 
very old  
DECISION  
Immediate steps be taken to reduce the arrears of c ases and to provide a speedy and 
efficient justice delivery system to the people by taking adequate measures, including 
suitably increasing the strength of Judges in High Courts and subordinate courts, filling 
up of existing vacancies at all levels on an urgent basis and by timely filling-up of the 
vacancies in future.  
ITEM NO. 4. INTRODUCTION OF SHIFT SYSTEM IN SUBORDINATE COURTS  
The Chief Justice of Gujarat High Court informed that the system of Evening Courts. 
had proved to be very successful in the state, more  than 62,000 cases were disposed 
by such courts in less than five months, and there was growing demand from various 
quarters for setting-up of such courts. Chief Justi ce of Andhra Pradesh High Court 
informed that in his State such courts were being r un in the morning and were quite 
successful in disposal of cases involving petty off ences. The Chief Justice of Delhi 
High Court informed that they were exploring introd uction of Evening Courts and 
had discussion with the Bar in this regard and he e xpected a positive outcome. The 
Chief Justice of Jharkhand High Court suggested shi ft courts in the evening since 
uninterrupted power supply was not available in the evening. A11 the States welcomed 
the introduction of shift system in subordinate cou rts and promised to work in that 
direction.  
DECISION  
Evening/morning courts to be set-up, wherever found feasible, and appropriate cases 
including those involving petty offences be transferred to such courts. Either retired 
Judicial Officers be re-employed or serving Judicial Officers be given suitable incentive, 
to preside over these Courts.  
ITEM NO. 5   ALTERNATE DISPUTE REDRESSAL MECHANISM  
There was consensus amongst the participants that r esolution of disputes through 
regular courts along, which was otherwise not congenial for a peaceful society, was 
not adequate to address the problem of huge backlog  of cases and therefore, it was 
necessary to resort to alternative modes of dispute s resolution, such as negotiation, 
mediation, conciliation and Lok Adalats. It was acknowledged that since the regular 
courts were already overburdened, it was necessary to train Advocates in ADR methods 
in mediation, conciliation and to entrust the task of settlement of disputes through 
alternative disputes redressal system to them.  
DECISION  
Alternative Dispute Redressal systems such as media tion, negotiation, conciliation 
and Lok Adalats be adequately strengthened so as to bring about a peaceful settlement 
to the disputes and as far as possible members of the bar alone be engaged as mediators 
and conciliators.

388. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be

2,89,86,205 cases are reported pending in the District & Subordinate Courts and the various 
High Courts as on 30.9.2007 out of which 37,00,223 cases are pending in the various High 
Courts. In the Supreme Court 46,926 cases are reported pending as on 31.12.2007.  
(b) and (c) With a view to making a substantial impact in reduction of arrears of pending 
cases in courts, the Government has introduced The Gram Nyayalays Bill, 2007' for 
establishing 5067 Gram Nyayalayas. This Bill will enable setting up of more trial courts in 
the country at the intermediate Pachayat level. These courts would provide justice in relatively 
ordinary civil and criminal cases to the rural population. The procedure to be followed by 
these courts has also been kept simple and flexible so that cases can be heard and disposed 
of within 90 days' period. It is also envisaged that these courts would be mobile and would 
hear the parties in their respective villages to achieve the goal of providing justice to the 
people at their doorsteps.

Participation of private sector for development of geo-thermal energy  
409. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH. Will the Minister of NEW AND RENEWABLE 
ENERGY be pleased to state:  
 whether the participation of private sector is encouraged in developing geo-thermal 
energy in the country; 
 if so, the details of support extended to the participants by the Government during the 
last three years, year-wise; 
 whether any location in the country has been identified to generate the energy; and 
 if so, the details thereof along with the measures taken to identify new locations in the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NEW AND RE NEWABLE 
ENERGY (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) and (b) The Ministry of New and Renewable 
Energy is encouraging participation of private sect or in all forms of renewable energy, 
including geo-thermal energy. The Ministry has encouraged the private sector participation 
in geo-thermal energy by allowing access to the data collected on geo-thermal resource in 
India by the National Geophysical Research Institut e (NGRI), Hyderabad through the 
Ministry's support. The Ministry also facilitates t he private sector to undertake their own 
investigations/assessment studies for geo-thermal energy and submission of Detailed Project 
Report (DPR) to the concerned State Government for exploitation of this resource.  
None has approached the Ministry for financial supp ort during the last three years for 
harnessing the geo-thermal energy.  
(c) and (d) Based on the studies carried out by NGRI so far, the Puga Valley in Ladakh in 
Jammu and Kashmir and Tatapani in Sarguja District of Chhattisgarh have been identified 
as potential sites for tapping the geo-thermal ener gy for power generation and thermal 
applications. Such studies are also in progress thr ough NGRI in Surajkund in Jharkhand, 
Badrinath-Tapovan in Uttarakhand and Satluj-Beas and Parvati Valleys in Himachal Pradesh.

Cooperation in power sector with Nepal and Bhutan 4 11. SHRI  
MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  
 whether Government is examining the possibility of tapping the resources available in 
the storage dams of Nepal and Bhutan to enhance energy supply; 
 if so, the details thereof; and 
 how much power is being imported from Bhutan and how much supply is likely to be 
increased? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
India and Nepal have agreed, under the 1996 Mahakal i Treaty, to jointly develop the 
Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project (5600 MW) on the M ahakali river, where it forms the 
border between the two countries. The two Governments are engaged in finalization of the 
Detailed Project Report (DPR) of the Pancheshwar Pr oject. On the Sun-Kosi Sapta Kosi 
Project (around 3300 MW), a Joint Project Office ha s been established in Nepal with 
Government of India funds to carry out field invest igation for preparation of the DPR. 
Preliminary discussions have also been held on the feasibility of Naumure Hydroelectric 
Project. In addition, Government of Nepal is taking  steps for development of hydropower 
projects in Nepal through foreign and domestic private investments.  
India has longstanding bilateral cooperation with B hutan in the Hydropower sector. 
Government of India has assisted construction of 336 MW Chukha, 60 MW Kurichhu and 
1020 MW Tala Hydroelectric Projects in Bhutan. In a ddition the Detailed Project Reports 
for two Storage Projects viz., Sunkosh (4060 MW) and Bunakha (180 MW) in Bhutan were 
prepared with the assistance of Government of India.  
An Inter-governmental Agreement has also been signed in July 2007 for the implementation 
of 1095 MW Punatsangchhu-I Hydroelectric Project in  Bhutan.  
(c) Currently, the Government of India is importing surplus power from Bhutan generated 
by Chukha (336 MW), Kurichhu (60 MW) and Tala (1020  MW) Hydroelectric Projects. 
During the period April, 2007 to January, 2008,5064 MU of energy has been imported from 
Bhutan. Under a bilateral Agreement signed in July, 2006, Government of India has agreed 
to purchase 5000 MW of power from Bhutan by the year 2020.

Delays in reforms in power sector  
417. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA:  
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  
(a) whether the Prime Minister has recently expressed concern over the delays in 
implementing power reforms in the country;  

Written Answers to  [3 MARCH, 2008]  Unstarred Questions   117  
 if so, the details thereof; 
 whether there is an abnormal delay in awarding mega  transmission projects and 
commissioning of Ultra Mega Power Projects resulting in shortfall in power generation; 
 if so, the details thereof; and 
 the steps taken by Government to implement the pending power projects and to boost 
the power generation capacity in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) Electricity 
is a concurrent subject under the Constitution. Therefore, the Government of India has been 
discussing power sector issues with the States from  time to time. Addressing the Chief 
Ministers in the Conference of Chief Ministers conv ened by the Ministry of Power on 
28th May, 2007, the Prime Minister expressed concern, inter alia, on the poor progress in 
the addition to generation capacity, in cutting down transmission and distribution losses, in 
reducing wasteful consumption, in providing open access and in attracting adequate private 
investment in power sector. A copy of the resolution adopted by the Conference expressing 
resolve of the Centre and the States to address various issues in the power sector is given at 
the Statement.  
(c) and (d) The selected developer of an Ultra Mega Power Project is allowed a specified 
period for commissioning the project beginning from the date on which the power purchase 
agreement becomes effective. Three Ultra Mega Power Projects for which the power purchase 
agreements have become effective, are slated to be commissioned during the Twelfth Five 
Year Plan. No deviation from the commissioning schedule as provided in the power purchase 
agreements has been reported so far.  
There is no project known as "Mega Transmission Project". However, the transmission 
systems for evacuation of power associated with Ult ra Mega Power Projects have been 
planned by Central Electricity Authority and are to  be implemented by POWERGRID 
matching with the commissioning schedule of the respective Ultra Mega Power Projects.  
(e) Following steps have been taken by the Government to ensure timely completion of 
Eleventh Plan projects:  
(i) Expediting Letters of Award (LoA) in respect of Eleventh Plan projects in the first 
year of the Eleventh Plan.  
(ii) Removal of constraints in meeting the main plant supplies for thermal projects, (iii) 
Addressing the issue related to availability of Balance of Plant (BoP) requirements, (iv) 
Overcoming shortage of manpower, (v) Regular monitoring of generation capacity 
addition targets.  
                             Statement Resolution adopted by the                                                                         
Chief Ministers'Conference on Power (28th May, 2007,)  
1. The Conference recognizes the vital importance of the power sector in the development 
of the economy which is on a trajectory of high gro wth and resolves that a time bound 
closely monitored action programme for accelerated capacity addition, drastic loss reduction, 
achievement of the rural electrification targets set out under Bharat Nirman, and promov of 
efficient energy and Demand Side Management, be put in place at the Centre and States.  
 

118    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
 The Conference acknowledges that electricity is a c oncurrent subject. The States and 
the Centre shall jointly endeavour to provide acces s to electricity to all. The States are 
conscious of their primary responsibility of ensuring availability and distribution of electricity. 
The continued proactive initiatives of the Union Go vernment in coordinated planning, 
supplementing generation through Central Public Sector Undertakings, inter-State and inter- ' 
region transmission, rural electrification, providi ng financial assistance through various 
programmes and institutions, and in guiding the ref orms process, along with the proactive 
stance of the States, are vital to achieve this objective.- 
 The Conference acknowledges that the Bharat Nirman targets for rural electrification 
have to be met in order to ensure that rural India has adequate access to electricity; and 
resolves that the Central Government would, through the Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran 
Yojana, continue to assist the State Governments help expand their rural networks and extend 
household connections to BPL families as set out under Bharat Nirman. The Government of 
India, in discharge of its statutory functions under the Electricity Act, would extend all possible 
financial and techno-managerial support. The States  would urgently formulate clear, cost 
effective and comprehensive rural electrification plans which would address the concerns of 
sustainability, availability, affordability and delivery of power. The States should also develop 
appropriate revenue and franchisee models that may use system improvements to meet the 
requirements of the rural areas and disadvantaged groups, particularly wherever it is a better 
alternative to existing arrangements. The Centre shall support the States in their commitment 
and take into account the special requirements of different States. 
 The Conference noted with concern that the country is presently facing serious peaking 
and energy shortages, and resolves that the States and the Centre would vigorously pursue 
the capacity addition programmes so as to create ca pacities in line with the rapid growth of . 
demand of electricity and eliminate shortages withi n the Eleventh Plan to ensure the goal of 
"Power for all by 2012". The Centre and the States would ensure timely placement of orders 
by December 2007 for all projects intended to give benefits during the Eleventh Plan and 
ensure regular monthly project monitoring for their  timely commissioning along pre-
determined milestones. The Centre would set up a Na tional Power Project Management 
Board for monitoring the timely commissioning of th e unprecedented capacity addition and 
associated transmission projects. The States would also set up similar dedicated apparatus. 
Immediate steps would also be taken to expedite the  development of hydro power and 
renewable sources. The Centre would continue to ens ure the timely development of inter-
State and inter-region transmission lines, with act ive facilitation by the States. Matching 
sub-transmission and distribution networks would be  created by the States to synchronize 
with the capacity addition. The States supported th e initiative of the Centre to set up Ultra 
Mega Power Projects (UMPPs). The Centre would also develop the necesary transmission 
network for UMPPs. The States would continue to eff ect further improvement in the PLF of 
their existing generating stations. The Government of India would facilitate the timely and < 
adequate availability of coal and gas for the gener ating plants at reasonable and competitive 
prices within the existing legal framework. The lin kage from coal fields will be locationally 
rationalized, to the extent possible. 
 The Conference recognizes that an estimated captive  generating capacity of about 
20,000 MW is being sub-optimally utilized in a phase of critical power shortage; and resolves 
that no generating capacity would be left idle. The  States would facilitate captive power 
plants to provide spare generating capacity to the grid and strive to do away with restrictive 
levies, duties and regulations in a time-bound manner. 

Written Answers to  [3 MARCH, 2008]  Unstarred Questions    119  
 The Conference further resolves that the States commit themselves to operationalizing 'open 
access' in the transmission and distribution sectors and resolve to issue policy directives to 
regulators, if necessary, to appropriately restructure cross subsidy surcharge, wheeling charges 
and other charges, with a view to augment the quantum of power flowing into the grid in the 
prevailing environment of shortages. 
 The Conference recognizes that the operationalizing of'open access' and competition in the 
supply of electricity to consumers would improve the supply position, help lower the tariffs and 
attract much needed investment in capacity addition; and resolved that the Centre and the States 
would unshackle generation, transmission and distri bution to enhance the availability of 
electricity and its unhindred movement to consumers. The Centre and the States would also 
issue any necessary policy directives to any undertaking or regulator to this end, in the interest of 
consumers, within and outside the concerned State. 
 The Conference recognizes that the current level of AT&C losses constitute a grave threat 
to the viability of the power sector and the distribution segment, which is currently losing about 
Rs. 47,000 crores per annum, is the weakest link in the power system; and resolves that the 
States commit themselves to achieve and sustain drastic reduction in the overall AT&C losses 
through the next five years, and at least to a level of 15% in the APDRP project areas as has been 
demonstrated by the participating States in 163 towns and cities. Towards this end, the States with 
appropriate assistance from the Centre would establish the necessary baseline data and IT 
applications for energy accounting and auditing, besides ensuring a resolute elimination of 
electricity theft, which is negating various investments and initiatives for power sector reforms. It 
is further reiterated that where free or subsidized power is provided to a section of consumers, the 
State Government shall ensure upfront payment of the same to the utilities. 
 The Conference recognizes that there is a very significant potential of saving electricity 
through its efficient use; and resolves that States and the Centre should focus on Demand Side 
Management measures and ensure such interventions as would provide immediate results for saving 
electricity. These interventions could include bulk procurement and distribution of CFLs, 
adoption of the Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC), promoting and mandating the use 
of energy efficient pump sets and other energy efficient equipment and appliances, besides giving 
appropriate financial and tax incentives for their manufacture. 
10. To periodically review the implementation of the resolutions adopted in the Conference, 
it is decided to set up a Standing Group of Power M inisters under the Chairmanship of the 
Union Power Minister to meet once a quarter.

Use  of clean coal technology in power sector  
420. SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  
 the steps taken to bring clean coal technology to the power sector; and 
 which are the countries from where this technology can be imported? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a ) Some of the 
prevalent clean coal technologies and steps being taken to adopt these technologies in India 
are as follows:  
(i) Supercritical Technology: —  
In India supercritical units of 660 MW are under installation at Sipat and Barn Thermal 
Power Stations (TPS) of NTPC Ltd. Apart from these,  a number of supercritical 
units with unit size of 660/800 MW have been planne d to be set up by NTPC Ltd. 
and State utilities. Ultra Mega Power Projects are also envisaged to be with 
supercritical parameters.  
(ii) Circulating Fluidised Bed Combustion (CFBC) Technol ogy: —  
Four CFBC units of 125 MW each are operating at Surat lignite TPS and Akrimota 
TPS in Gujarat. Six CFBC units of 125 MW each are under execution at Surat Lignite, 
Giral TPS and Barsingsar TPS. CFBC units of 250 MW are being installed at Neyvelli 
by Neyvelli Lignite Corporation.  
(iii) Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle (IGCC)  
So far the world over, IGCC technology has been adopted for low ash coal which is 
not suitable for Indian high ash coal. In India, ef forts are underway to develop this 
technology through indigenous efforts.  
(b) Supercritical generating units are being manufactured by a number of countries viz., 
USA, Japan, Germany, Korea, Russia, China etc. BHEL has also on-going collaboration for 
manufacture of supercritical boilers and turbine generators with M/s Alstom and M/s Siemens 
respectively. M/s Larsen & Toubro Limited (L&T) has also formed a joint venture company 
for manufacture of supercritical boilers and turbine generators with M/s Mitsubishi,Heavy 
Industries (MHI), Japan.  
CFBC boilers are already being manufactured in Indi a and BHEL has been supplying 
boilers and turbine generators for 125 MW and 250 M W supercritical units installed by 
power utilities.

Power demand in Maharashtra  
422. SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  
 whether Maharashtra Government is currently facing a daily power shortage of 4000 to 
5000 MW, which is expected to be over 10,000 M W by the end of the Eleventh Five Year Plan; 
 whether the Minister has convened a special review meeting in Mumbai to discuss the 
current demand and supply mismatch, proposed genera tion capacity and has decided to 
review the time schedule promised by Bharat Heavy E lectricals Limited for the supply of 
power plants and equipments for the timely completion of Maha Genco's proposed capacity 
addition; and 
 to what extent the power shortage in the State has been reduced? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) During the period 
April, 2007 to January, 2008, the energy shortage in Maharashtra was 16,289 MU (17.2%) 
and the peak shortage was 4844 MW (26.4%). Accordin g to the anticipated power supply 
position worked out by the Central Electricity Auth ority on the basis of demand forecast 
made in the 17th Electric Power Survey and the capa city addition programmed during the 
Eleventh Five Year Plan, the energy requirement in Maharashtra is likely to be met in full 
but the State is likely to face peaking shortage of  3532 MW (16.1%) at the end of 
Eleventh Plan (2011-12).  
 Review meetings are convened by the Central Electricity Authority, Ministry of Power 
as well as at the level of Minister of Power from time to time to discuss the prevailing power 
supply position and the measures required to expedite completion of on-going power projects. 
 The energy and peaking shortage in Maharashtra during the current year (April, 2007 to 
January, 2008) have marginally reduced to 17.2% and  26.4% respectively as compared to 
17.4% and 26.7% during the corresponding period of last year (April, 2006 to January, 2007).

 the steps being taken by Central/State Government to fill this gap? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a ) and (b) During 
the period April, 2007 to January, 2008, the daily energy requirement of Rajasthan was of 
the order of 97 Million Units and the maximum requirement of power in Rajasthan was of 
the order of 6374 MW.  
The existing installed generating capacity of the S tate Sector and Private Sector Power 
Stations in the State of Rajasthan is about 4518 MW .  
(c) The power requirements of a State is met from i ts own generation, allocation from 
central sector generating stations and import of power from other States. The main reasons  

Written Answers to  [3 MARCH, 2008]  Unstarred Questions    129  
for shortage of power in various States, including the State of Rajasthan is inadequate capacity 
addition vis-a-vis growth in demand. During the period April, '07 to January, '08 Rajasthan 
faced energy and peaking shortages of 1.8% and 12.8 % as compared to 5.1% and 16.8% 
respectively during the corresponding period of last year. As compared to 6.5% increase in 
energy requirement during the above period, the increase in availability was 12.2%, which 
helped in reducing the gap between demand and suppl y of power.  
(d) Electricity being a concurrent subject under the Constitution, supply and distribution 
of electricity to different areas/various categorie s of consumers in a State falls within the 
purview of the concerned State Government/Power Uti lities. The Government of India 
supplements the efforts of State Governments by way  of generation capacity addition and 
bulk transmissionof power through the Central Sector Power Utilities.  
The steps taken/being taken to improve power supply  position in the country include 
augmentation of generating capacity by over 78,500 MW during the 11th Plan, development 
of Ultra Mega Power Projects of 4,000 MW capacity, improving performance of existing 
power stations, renovation, modernization and life extension of old and inefficient generating 
units, harnessing surplus captive power into the grid, strengthening of inter-state and inter-
regional transmission capacity for optimum utilization of available power promoting demand 
side management, energy efficiency and energy conservation measures and import of power 
from Bhutan.  
Capacity addition to the tune of 1790 MW has been e nvisaged in the State Sector in 
Rajasthan during the Eleventh Plan.

NTPC's Joint venture for equipment manufacturing  
425. SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN: 
SHRI MOHAMMED AMIN:  
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  

130 Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
 whether NTPC has decided to form a joint venture with M/s Bharat Forge for equipment 
manufacturing; 
 if so, the details of the proposal approved by NTPC, including stake holding, product 
profile and quantum of investment, etc.; 
 whether NTPC has bagged any order for UMPP projects; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 whether NTPC's entry in capital goods industry is to shift from its core area of activity 
in power generation; and 
 if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a ) and (b) NTPC 
has signed en MoU with M/s Bharat Forge Limited on 8/2/2008 to promote a Joint Venture 
(JV) Company.  
The Company is proposed to be set up with equity participation from NTPC and Bharat 
Forge Limited in the ratio 49.51 respectively. The proposed authorized capital of the company 
is Rs. 10 lakhs. However, the investment in future will depend upon the techno-commercial 
viability of the proposal.  
The aim of the JV company is to establish a facility, subject to techno-commercial viability, 
to initially take up manufacture of castings, forgings, fittings and high pressure pipings required 
for power and other industries, Balance of Plant (BoP) equipment for the power sector etc., 
including tie ups with strategic partners. The JV c ompany may eventually also explore 
opportunities related to manufacturing of power equipment.  
(c) and (d) No, Sir. NTPC has not bagged any order for Ultra Mega Power Project (UMPP) 
till date.  
(e) and (0 No, Sir. NTPC does not plan to shift fro m its core area of activity in power 
generation. However, in order to strengthen its com petive advantage in Power Generation 
Business, NTPC plans to strategically diversify its portfolio to emerge as an integrated power 
major and accordingly continuously explores various business opportunities. At present it 
does not have the necessary expertise to undertake power equipment manufacturing activities 
on its own. Therefore, NTPC plans to partner with suitable strategic partners who can bring 
the expertise in manufacturing which in combination  with NTPC's strength in Planning, 
Engineering, Project Management and Operational expertise can be used to develop a viable 
equipment manufacturing facility apart from providing services.

Setting up of UMPPs  
429. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:  
 whether it is a fact that Government has not been able to identify the sites of 10 Ultra Mega 
Power Projects (UMPPs) that were proposed to be set -up; 
 if so, the reasons therefor; 
 the number of cases in which sites for such projects have, so far, been identified and bids 
from private companies, etc., invited and finalized with the. details of each case; and 
 the action proposed in finalizing other such Projects during 2008-09? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (d) After finalization 
of sites in consultation with the States, bidding process has been initiated in respect of four Ultra 
Mega Power projects (UMPPs). Out of these four, bidding process in respect of UMPPs to be 
located in Sasan (Madhya Pradesh), Mundra (Gujarat) and Krishnapatnam (Andhra Prdesh) has 
been completed and the Special Purpose Vehicles have been tansferred to Reliance Power Limited 
in respect of Sasan and Krishnapatnam UMPPs and to Tata Power Company Limited in respect of 
Mundra UMPP, being the successful developers identified through tariff based competitive 
bidding process. The bidding process in respect of the fourth project namely, Tillaiya UMPP is 
currently in progress.

Among the remaining projects, Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has identified a suitable 
site for setting up of an UMPP in Orissa in consultation with the State Government. However,

been short listed in consultation with the State Government.

Review of power projects  
432. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Minister of POWER be  pleased to state:  
 whether some of the power projects in the country have not performed properly during 
the last five years; 
 if so, whether Government proposes to review their performance and being forward 
some amendments particularly in the Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY) 
and Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP); and 
 if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHlL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) The performance 
of power plants is accessed/gauged in terms of actu al generation vis-a-vis their generation 
target. The generation tagets are fixed for the power station on a year to year basis, keeping 
in view their installed capacity, age of the units,  past performance, planned outages, likely 
availability of water/fuel (both quantity and quality) etc. While availability of water during 
monsoon and non-monsoon season as well as irrigation requirements influence performance 
of hydro power station, the quality and availability of fuel have a bearing on the performance 
of thermal power stations. Therefore, the actual generation achieved by some power plants 
including old power plants in the state sector is at variation with the target.  
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir, the performance of power stat ions is being reviewed by competent 
authorities.

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (c) Accoding to the 
information available with the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), the generation capacity of Captive 
Power Plants (CPP) of capacity more than 1 MW was 21468 MW as on 31.3.2006 and 22335 M W 
as on 31.3.2007. During the year 2005-06,5364.74 Million Units of electricity have been exported 
by these CPPs to the utilities. No sanction is required under the provisions of the Electricity Act, 
2003 for setting up captive power plants.  
(d) and (e) Government has taken various legislative, policy and administrative measures to 
facilitate captive generation and utilization of surplus capacity.  
Under the Electricity Act, 2003, captive power plants, including group captive, have been 
freely permitted. The Act provides that any person may construct, maintain or operate a captive 
generating plant and dedicated transmission lines. Under the provisions of the Act, every person, 
who has constructed a captie generating plant and maintains and operates such plant, shall have the 
right to open access for the purposes of carrying electricity from his captive generating plant to 
the destination of this use subject to the availability of transmission capacity.  
National Electricity Policy, notified in February, 2005, emphasizes the need for bringing 
surplus capacity available with a large number of captive and standby generating stations in India 
to the grid continuously or durting certain time periods.  
Tariff Policy, notified in January, 2006, recognizes that captive generation is an important means 
to make competitive power available and urges the Electricity Regulatory Commission to creat an 
enabling environment that encourages captive plants to be connected to the grid.  
The conference of Chief Ministers, on power sector,  held in May, 2007, under the 
chairmanship of the Prime Minister, has resolved to facilitate captive power plants to provide the 
spare generating capacity to the grid and strive to do away with restrictive levies, duties and 
regulations in a time bound manner.

Statement  
Measures to put a check on the atrocities against women and children  
Law and order and other criminal matters in a State  subject under the Constitution and 
therefore, the direct responsibility for dealing with enforcement of the concerned Acts is that 
of the State Governments and the mechanisms under them. The registration, investigation, 
detection and prevention of crimes against women is primarily the responsibility of the State 
Governments/UT Administrations. However, the Government of India has initiated a number 
of measures to check such crimes, such as:—  
Enacted the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 which provides for 
more effective protection of the Constitutional Rights of women, who are victims of violence 
of any kind occurring within the family including any unlawful demand for dowry.  
Setting up of helplines for women in distress under the Swadhar Scheme.  
Support services to victims of violence through schemes such as Short Stay Homes and 
Swadhar under which shelter, maintenance, counselin g, capacity building, occupational 
training, medical aid and other services are provided.  
A scheme has been formulated on 13.11.2007 to change the mindset of the society towards 
the girl child and view her as an asset and not a burden, namely, "Conditional Cash Transfer 
with Insurance Cover Scheme". The scheme provides for cash transfers to family of the girl 
child (preferably the mother) on fulfilling certain conditionalities such as birth and registration 
of the girl child, immunization, enrolment to school; retention in school, delaying the marriage 
age beyond 18 years. Insurance cover is also proposed for the girl child as a safety net and to 
enable the girl to receive a lump sum at the age of 18 years.  
Launching of a comprehensive scheme under the name "Ujjawala" on 4.12.2007 for 
victims of trafficking and commercial sexual exploitation. The scheme has five components 
— Prevention, Rescue, Rehabilitation, Re-integratio n and Repatriation.  
Redressal of grievances through interventions of Na tional and State Commissions for 
Women.  
Organizing legal Literacy and Legal Awareness Camps. 
Implementation of schemes for (i) awareness generation and advocacy and (ii) economic 
empowerment of women through the programmes of Rash triya Mahila Kosh, Swashakti 
project, Swayamsidha Project, Swawlamban Programme and Support to Training and 
Employment Programme (STEP).  
Review of laws with a view to remove provisions which may be discriminatory to women 
and to enhance punishments for crimes against women.  
Sensitization of judiciary and police and civil administration on gender issues.  
Follow up of reports of cases of atrocities against women received from various sources, 
including NCW, with concerned authorities in the Central and the State Governments.  
Apart from legislative changes in the relevant Acts , instructions/guidelines have been 
issued to the State Governments/Union Territory Adm inistrations to effectively enforce 
legislation relating to crimes against women and monitor the enforcement and to give more 
focused attention to improving the administration of criminal justice system and to take such

measures as are necessary for the prevention of crime against women and other vulnerable 
sections of society. The measures suggested include:

 the food being given to the pregnant women, breast feeding women and children upto

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and (b) As per the guidelines 
contained in the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) Scheme, the State 
Government/Union Territory Administrations have the flexibility to select the type of food 
to be provided as supplementary nutrition to Pregnant and Lactating Mothers and children 
below six years of age. It could be milk, pre-processed or semi-processed food or food

of 300 calories and 10 gms. of proteins per child, 500 calories and 15-20 gms. of proteins 
per pregnant woman/nursing mother, and 600 calories and 20 gms. of proteins per severly 
malnourished child be provided for 300 days in a year.

Lactating mothers and children below 6 years of age coming to the Anganwadi Centre.

concern. Malnutrition is a multifaceted problem, the determinants of which vary from food 
insecurity, female illiteracy, poor access to health-care, safe drinking water, sanitation and 
poor purchasing power. Early marriages of girls, teenage pregnancies resulting in low birth

from Assam State Government, the Assam State Commis sioner for women registered 31  
cases relating to trafficking on women and the police remanded 12 girl victims of trafficking  
• to the State Home for Women, Guwahati for custodial care.  
(b) and (c) The Assam State Government has reported  that it has stepped up vigilance 
action by police to stop trafficking on women. The State Home for Women under Social 
Welfare Department has been equipped to take custodial care of victims of women trafficking, 
training, counseling and generation of community aw areness. Victims lodged in the State 
Home are also restored to parents/guardians suitably. As a long-term measures the victims in 
the State Homes are extended facilities of training and education for eventual restoration to 
society.  
The Ministry of Women and Child Development, Government of India is implementing 
the scheme of Ujjawala wherein rehabilitation of victims of trafficking is provided through 
Shelter, Food, Clothing, Counselling, Medical and l egal aid and Vocational training. In 
addition, the Ministry also runs Swadhar Shelter Homes, which is a Scheme for women in 
difficult circumstances which includes victims of trafficking.

465. SHRI VIJAYJ DARDA:  
SHRIGIREESH KUMAR SANGHI:  
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
 whether Government is aware of the findings of the UNICEF Report 'Programme for 
Children' released in 2nd week of December, 2007 th at malnutrition and child mortality 
continues to endanger the lives of children in India; and 
 if so, how 8.3 million such Indian children will ge t even semblance of food items 
having adequate nutrition, to begin with the gradually assuring full nutrition by the end of 
Eleventh Five Year Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD  
. DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) As per a statistical review  
report of UNICEF for a World Fit for Children titled "Progress for Children" the rate of  
underweight prevalence in children in India under five years for the period 2000-2006 was  
,43% and under five years mortality rate for 2006 was 76 per thousand live births.  
(b) Ministry of Women and Child Development is impl ementing the Integrated Child 
Development Services Scheme with a package of servi ces for supplementary nutrition, 
immunization, health check-up, referral services, p re-school non-formal education and 
nutrition & health education. 62.96 million children in the age group of 6 months to 6 year 
received supplementary nutrition under the Scheme as on 30th September 2007. The number 
of such children are likely to increase in the Eleventh Plan..
